contentHtml:
Practical standards for building understandable, accessible and efficient interfaces when a project has limited or no dedicated UX and design support. Use them for web application screens, registration flows and internal tools.

UX Position

The user should be able to answer five questions throughout a journey:

  1. Where am I and which task can I complete here?
  2. What information or decision is needed from me?
  3. What will happen if I take this action?
  4. What happened, and has my work been saved or completed?
  5. How can I correct, leave, recover or continue?

The underlying decision strategy is to understand the task, remove unnecessary work, make choices predictable and keep outcomes observable. Visual polish supports this strategy; it cannot establish whether the right task was built.

Decision Priorities

When requirements compete, use this local order and record material tradeoffs:

  1. Protect access, user intent, data and consequential decisions.
  2. Make the main task understandable and completable.
  3. Prevent mistakes and make recovery possible.
  4. Reduce repeated effort, waiting and memory demands.
  5. Improve visual consistency and presentation.

Accessibility applies throughout these priorities. Efficiency means successful completion with reasonable effort, including correction; a smaller click count alone is not a success criterion.

Starting Without A Designer

  • Identify the people, task, context and constraints before composing screens.
  • Reuse the product's existing design system and interaction patterns. Where none exists, choose a maintained accessible component foundation that fits the application and define a small consistent set of tokens and patterns.
  • Write a short journey/screen brief within the feature specification.
  • Implement the primary path plus failure, interruption and recovery states.
  • Review with the checklist and observe representative people doing real tasks; record assumptions when user access is unavailable.

These standards provide a working baseline. Specialist input is valuable when research uncertainty, accessibility barriers, high-consequence decisions or complex workflows remain unresolved. A heuristic review is not user research.

Navigation

Document Use when
Journeys and Decisions Defining the task, reducing steps and choosing a flow
Screen Structure and Content Organizing information, navigation, actions, lists and language
Forms and Data Entry Creating records, editing information or registering accounts
Feedback and Recovery Defining saving, errors, pending work, retries and destructive actions
Accessibility Implementing keyboard, assistive technology and responsive behavior
Evaluation and Validation Checking task completion and learning from actual use
UX Checklist Reviewing a screen or journey before delivery
References Understanding source guidance and local adaptations

Start with the Screen and Journey Brief and the Customer Registration Example.

Non-Negotiable Defaults

  • A user-facing workflow MUST identify its user goal and completion condition.
  • Actions MUST communicate their scope and material consequences.
  • A consequential operation MUST distinguish requested, pending, completed, failed and unknown outcomes wherever those states can occur.
  • Forms MUST justify required information, expose labels and instructions, retain appropriate input after errors and offer a correction path.
  • Critical journeys MUST support keyboard use and accessible names, roles, states and feedback; production web interfaces target WCAG 2.2 level AA.
  • Error handling MUST protect against avoidable data loss and duplicate effects. A disabled button alone does not guarantee this protection.
  • Validation evidence MUST distinguish automated checks, human review and observed usability sessions. Unperformed checks remain unverified.

In this book, MUST denotes a required local control; SHOULD denotes a default that can be adapted with a reason. WCAG requirements and heuristic guidance are identified separately in the references.

Applying This Standard With Codex

Read the entry point and relevant topic documents before changing a screen. Inspect the existing product conventions, specification and components. Use known business rules; record missing rules rather than inventing requirements for personal data, permissions or consequential transactions.

Suggested implementation request:

Apply ux/README.md and ux/ux-checklist.md to this screen or journey.
Identify the user, task and completion condition. Reuse existing components.
Define fields, actions, states and recovery before implementation. Cover
keyboard use, mobile layout, validation, saving and server failure. Verify the
implemented behavior and report evidence, assumptions and remaining gaps.

A small change can keep its brief in the existing issue or specification. Use a separate record only when it helps maintain the decisions.

Related Standards

  • Human outcomes: Users First.
  • Behavior contracts: Spec-Driven Development.
  • Languages and formatting: Internationalization and Localization.
  • Regression evidence: Testing Standards.
  • Data, permissions and credentials: Security Standards.
  • Reliable completion: SRE Standards.
